title: The Red Carpet
reviewNotes: All 29 diagrams/captions reviewed; native initial board has White Kg3/Rc6/Nd4/f4/g5/h6 against Kh5/Bh7/Rb2/b4/c2/d3. Nf5 finite proof covers all twelve legal replies. After Bxf5/h7 all seventeen replies are covered, including Bg6/Be6 blocks and four c-pawn promotions. Four teaching branches show source clearance, independent promotion and both bishop blocks. No uniqueness or Ne6 draw claim is certified.
transcript: Some chess.com puzzles are just incredible. It seems like there is no way to stop black from getting a new queen. Black is just going to be playing D2 and D1 or rook to B1 and pawn to C1 and promote. But you might notice that this black king is kind of trapped by the white pieces. So it means that we can use the knight to create a checkmating one threat by either going to A5 or to E6. At first, it might seem like going to E6 with the intention of delivering this checkmate is the safest option. But actually this cuts the communication of the rook with the G6 square. And believe it or not, if black is brave enough, he can walk out with king to G6 allowing a discovered check by the rook. But since black always has the threat of getting the new queen, this is at best going to be a draw. So incredibly, the only winning move is knight to F5 with the same idea of going to G7 with a checkmate. But of course, this doesn't seem to make a lot of sense because the bishop can just capture the knight. So the question is, what have we achieved? The position hasn't changed at all. But you see, the position has changed. We have freed up the H7 square. And now white can start walking up with the pawn and try to get a new queen of his own. But again, some of you might think, wait, can't the bishop just come back and capture that pawn? But you see, both knight to F5 and pawn to H7 were what we call a clearance sacrifice because by removing those pieces, we have now created a beautiful red carpet for the rook to fly into H6 and deliver checkmate.
